pricing.freeTierCaps: $0 Trial; 50 credits, 100 recipients, 1 email warm-up slot, renews every 30 days; 50 free enrichment tokens also offered.
pricing.billingTerms: monthly, 3-month (-5%) and annual (up to 40% promo / 25% table discount) options shown; LinkedIn annual saves $7/slot/month
pricing.hiddenCosts: LinkedIn automation slots are not included in Sales Suite and cost $69/mo or $62/mo annual per slot; enrichment tokens cost $0.02/token and expire after 90 days; 1 prospect/email verification/company view costs 1 credit; deliverability checks cost 25 credits.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Snov.io, sequence permissioned contacts and enrich only through user-supplied providers. The hard boundary is proprietary contact discovery, verification credits, warm-up, and sales tooling, plus proprietary data, deliverability, and network effects.
coreLoopDIY: Import a permissioned lead list, enrich contacts only through user-supplied providers, personalize a modest sequence, enforce sending limits, and track replies without supplying proprietary contact data.
whatYouLose: proprietary contact discovery, verification credits, warm-up, and sales tooling
moatNotes: proprietary data, deliverability, and network effects
ongoingBurden: consent records, suppression lists, DNS, bounces, reputation, abuse complaints, provider limits, and changing email rules
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Snov.io because the durable value is accurate contact data and deliverability infrastructure; a sequence editor alone is not the product. The recurring cost buys consent records, suppression lists, DNS, bounces, reputation, abuse complaints, provider limits, and changing email rules, not just the visible interface.

rejectedAlternatives.name: listmonk
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A fine newsletter sender, but it does not watch replies and stop a sales sequence; wrong kind of email automation.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Mautic
rejectedAlternatives.desc: It can run the sequence, but it does not enrich contacts through user-supplied providers without custom integration work.

rejectedAlternatives.name: n8n
rejectedAlternatives.desc: It can wire enrichment APIs together, which is precisely the building project this list excludes.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Starter plan and a small permission-based outreach console DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Snov.io in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and a user-chosen transactional email provider; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: import a permissioned lead list, enrich contacts only through user-supplied providers, personalize a modest sequence, enforce sending limits, and track replies without supplying proprietary contact data.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Accept CSV imports only after the user confirms lawful collection and records the source.
Provide contact fields, tags, suppression status, consent notes, and a complete change history.
Build a short email sequence with delays, business-hour windows, and per-domain rate limits.
Use the configured provider for sends and process delivery, bounce, complaint, and unsubscribe webhooks.
Stop sequences immediately on reply, bounce, complaint, suppression, or manual pause.
Show deliverability warnings, daily send totals, and a mandatory preview before activation.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out scraping protected platforms.
Deliberately leave out buying or generating personal contact data.
Deliberately leave out automated inbox warm-up networks and evasion of provider limits.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
